_comment: What each measurement is allowed to cost, on a thesis-shaped project:
forty source files, two megabytes of LaTeX, a populated build directory
and a .git with a working tree.  These are budgets, not records -- the
point is to notice a regression, not to celebrate a number.  Anything
that goes over prints what it measured and exits nonzero.
bundle.initial_kb was raised from 760 to 775 when spell checking was
added: the switch, the settings row and the editor's side of it are
about four kilobytes that ship whether or not anyone turns it on. The
checker itself and its 98 kB word list are not in this number and are
not supposed to be -- they are fetched the first time the setting is
switched on and never otherwise, which is the whole reason a word list
this size is affordable at all.
Raised again from 775 to 782 by the hardening run, and in that order:
six kilobytes were taken *out* first, by fetching the upload card, the
paper chooser and the file view when they are wanted rather than before
anything draws, which is what makes this a budget for added value and
not a budget that gave way to drift. What went in: an error message
that is a stack rather than one string, a focus trap in the dialogs, a
shared throttling helper, and about ninety LaTeX commands the
completion list did not have -- a writer reached for textcolor and was
offered nothing at all. The last of those is most of it, and it is data
rather than code: the honest way back under 775 is to split the
settings card out of its always-visible trigger, which is a refactor
and not an import change, and it is not done.
Not raised a third time.  The budget was breached, and by less than it
looked: 786.3 against 782.  The 805 that was reported is vite's own
console figure, which counts a kilobyte as a thousand bytes, and this
number counts it as 1024 -- so a reading taken off the build output is
not this measurement and should not be compared with it.  What closed
the 4.3 kB was fetching the version panel when somebody asks for it,
the way the tutorial, the PDF pane and the share sheet already are:
it is behind a click, most sessions never open it, and the strip that
says you are viewing an old version comes with it in the same chunk
because it is only reachable through the panel.  779.1 now.
Raised from 782 to 800 by the agent panel rework, and the reason it
is a raise rather than a shave is worth writing down. What went in: a
permission control with three positions instead of a switch, the
confirmation that stands in front of the quietest one, a fourth answer
on the card, the turn plan that TodoWrite was already sending and the
panel was throwing away, an elapsed counter, per-call durations, and
the activity slice that replaced a backwards walk over the whole
transcript on every render. That last one gave some back: it deleted
code as well as adding it, and it is a saving on the streaming path
rather than only in bytes.
Nothing else was taken out first, which breaks the pattern the entries
above set, and the honest reason is that the cheap extractions have
already been done: the settings sheet, the tutorial, the PDF pane, the
share sheet, the paper chooser, the file view and the version panel are
all fetched on a click already. What is left in the entry chunk that
could leave it is the permission card and the four controls under the
composer, and the card is the wrong candidate: a session with an agent
in it sees cards, so it would be paying for a lazy chunk it always
loads plus a frame where the card is not drawn yet. The controls are a
real candidate and it is a refactor rather than an import change, and
it is not done.
800 rather than 790, deliberately, because the same rework still has
the selection toolbar, the plot affordances and image attachments to
come, and a budget raised three times in one run is a budget nobody
believes. If those land under 800 the number stays; if they do not, the
next reader should be suspicious rather than raising it again.
And the reason it could drift at all is that nothing routine looked.
This lived only in the benchmark tier, which is a minute of LaTeX on a
synthetic thesis and is run by hand.  The bundle needs none of that --
it is a property of frontend/dist -- so `bench.bench --bundle-only`
now runs inside scripts/check.sh --all, straight after the build that
produces the thing it measures.
project.open_ms is what a writer waits for when they click a project
in the list: the tree walk, the transcript, and the dependency scan
that decides what else could be previewed.  It was measured before
anything was changed, at 125 ms on a thesis, and every millisecond of
it was on the event loop -- so for that eighth of a second nobody
else's autosave, event stream or collaborator socket made progress.
It is 95 ms now, and off the loop.  The saving is the scan pruning
directories as it descends rather than listing everything with rglob
and filtering afterwards, which had it walking the whole of .git and
the whole build directory on a path a person waits for.
The budget is well above both numbers on purpose.  It exists to
notice this growing back, not to hold a record, and it is a walk over
a filesystem: a cold cache is a different machine from a warm one.
collab.* were added with peer-to-peer collaboration.  Both are on the
keystroke path: an edit arriving from a collaborator is an apply_update,
and every edit that settles becomes a write to disk.  Opening a document
is the cost of the first keystroke in a file, once per file per session.
collab.edit_to_disk_ms was added by the hardening run to settle a
finding rather than to guard a number.  The flush that writes a settled
edit back was described as expensive -- a sha256, a zlib pass over the
whole file, a log rewrite, four regex passes -- and it is all of those
things and it measures at about a tenth of a millisecond on a thesis,
against an ingest of three.  The budget is set well above both because
the point of having it is to notice that changing, not to hold a
record.  It runs with no session attached, so the version record is not
in it; history.record_ms is the rest and is about two milliseconds.
